questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Career opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Honestly, the biggest reason was Munich itself. It's one of the top tech hubs in Europe, with companies like BMW, Siemens, Google, and Apple all nearby. I wanted to be in a place where I could not only study but also get close to cutting-edge technology and explore internship opportunities alongside my studies.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. TUM's website covered most of what I needed before arriving, and the rest was filled in through orientation sessions once I got there.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: TUM had dedicated events and guidance for exchange students, which were announced both on their website and during in-person welcome meetings. There was a general orientation, departmental intros, and some social activities to help us settle in and meet other students. It made the first few weeks a lot less overwhelming.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Honestly, it was really difficult. As someone who doesn't speak German and wasn't planning to stay in Munich long-term, finding a place was a huge challenge. I arrived during the peak enrollment season, so demand was extremely high, prices were crazy, and most listings required a minimum one-year contract — which doesn't work for exchange students. It would really help if the host institution could guarantee housing, or at least offer more support for short-term stays.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Start looking as early as possible — seriously, the moment you get your acceptance. Be prepared for high rents and a very competitive market, especially at the start of the semester. A lot of landlords prefer long-term tenants and German speakers, so short-term options are limited and you might need to compromise on location or budget. If you can find a sublet or a spot in a shared flat (WG), that's usually the easiest route.

Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: TUM offers three main types of courses: lectures, practical courses, and seminars. Lectures use a regular registration process and usually don't have strict deadlines — you can just sign up when the time comes. Practical courses and seminars, however, work through a matching platform where you have to register much earlier, since spots are limited. The good news is the school sends out emails about it, so as long as you keep an eye on your inbox, you won't miss the deadline.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The course registration website has detailed instructions, and there are also in-person orientation sessions where everything gets explained step by step. Between the two, it's easy to figure out what you need to do.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Pretty successful overall. Once I understood the timing for the matching platform, I was able to get into the practical courses and seminars I was interested in, and the lectures were straightforward to sign up for.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Definitely look into the practical courses and seminars — they're small-class and often cover cutting-edge topics, which is a great experience you don't always get from regular lectures. Just remember they require early registration through a matching platform, so check your TUM emails carefully and don't miss the deadlines. For lectures, you can relax a bit since registration is more flexible.

questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The overall difficulty was reasonable — slightly more challenging than courses at KU, but very manageable. Lectures felt similar in workload, while practical courses and seminars tended to be a bit more demanding because they involve hands-on group work over the whole semester.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Lectures are pretty similar in format to KU. The main difference is the practical courses and seminars — they're essentially like KU projects, but pre-defined by the professors and done in groups. You don't propose your own topic; instead you join a structured project alongside other students, which makes the collaboration aspect much more central.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Honestly, I'd recommend any of the practical courses and seminars TUM offers — they're small-class, hands-on, and a great chance to work on cutting-edge topics together with other students. From my own experience, I particularly recommend the Master Lab Course – Applications in NLP and Responsible AI. Both gave me solid exposure to current research directions and were a nice mix of theory and practical work. If you want to make the most of your exchange academically, these kinds of courses are where you'll get the most out of TUM.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The biggest one was housing. Affordable places near the city center were extremely rare, and very few landlords offered six-month contracts, so I ended up living further out than I'd planned. Even then, rent took up a much bigger share of my budget than I expected.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Public transport was much cheaper than I thought, especially with the student/Deutschlandticket options — getting around Munich and even traveling around Germany was very affordable. Groceries and food prices were roughly similar to what I was used to in Copenhagen, so no big surprises there. Housing, on the other hand, was the one category that was noticeably more expensive than expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: TUM offers a pretty wide range of student activities, including university sports (ZHS), student clubs, and various cultural and social events organized for international students. Honestly, since I'm not originally from Denmark either, most things in Germany already felt new and interesting to me, so I didn't seek out specific "cultural" activities — just exploring daily life in Munich was enough.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: To be honest, I didn't really get involved in the sports or club side of things, so I don't have much to recommend there. What I'd suggest instead is going to the welcome events and exchange student meetups early on — that's where you'll naturally meet people and form your initial circle of friends.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Definitely make full use of the Deutschlandticket — it's one of the best deals you'll find as a student in Germany. For a low monthly price, you can take regional trains and public transport across the entire country, which makes weekend trips super easy. I'd recommend visiting places like Berlin, Hamburg, the Black Forest, Neuschwanstein Castle, and the Bavarian Alps. Munich itself is also a great base for day trips to Salzburg or smaller Bavarian towns. Honestly, the travel opportunities are one of the best parts of doing an exchange in Germany.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Honestly, I spent most of my time focused on my internship, so my exposure to local culture was fairly limited. From what I did experience, daily life in Munich felt easy enough to adapt to — things are well-organized and most people speak some English.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I don't have a lot of advice here, since my own social life was mostly tied to work rather than student circles. That said, joining the welcome events and exchange student activities early on is probably the easiest entry point.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Nothing major stood out to me. The language barrier was occasionally a small inconvenience in everyday situations, but otherwise I didn't run into any cultural differences that were hard to deal with.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I appreciated how organized and efficient everyday life is in Germany — public transport, services, and general infrastructure all just work. Munich also has a nice balance between city life and easy access to nature, which I really liked.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Start looking for housing as early as possible. Munich's rental market is extremely competitive and expensive, especially around the start of the semester, and most listings require a one-year contract. Don't underestimate this — it was by far the hardest part of my exchange.
- Don't miss the early course registration deadlines. Practical courses and seminars at TUM use a matching platform that opens well before the semester starts. Keep an eye on your TUM emails so you don't miss out — these courses are some of the best things TUM has to offer.
- Get the Deutschlandticket. It's cheap, lets you travel across all of Germany on regional transport, and turns every weekend into a potential adventure.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Munich is a fantastic base if you're interested in tech and engineering — there are tons of internship opportunities at companies like BMW, Siemens, Google, and Apple, so it's worth looking into combining your exchange with a part-time internship. Also, while many people in Munich speak English, knowing even a little German makes daily life noticeably smoother, especially when dealing with housing and administrative tasks.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Definitely the academic and professional exposure. The practical courses and seminars at TUM gave me hands-on experience with cutting-edge topics, and being in Munich opened up internship opportunities I wouldn't have had access to otherwise. Getting to combine high-quality coursework with real industry experience was exactly what I'd hoped for going into the exchange.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Finding housing, without question. As someone who doesn't speak German and only needed a place for one semester, the rental market was a real struggle — high prices, long-term contract requirements, and arriving during peak season made it incredibly difficult. It would help a lot if the host institution could offer more support or guaranteed housing for short-term exchange students.

questions.answer: Yes
